title: Roads and Libraries
directAnswer: Group cities into connected components from the road list, then decide each component independently. Inside a component of size s you must place at least one library; the cheapest way to reach all s cities is either s libraries (s × c_lib) or one library plus s − 1 roads (c_lib + (s − 1) × c_road). Take the per-component minimum and sum. Union-Find finds the components in O(E · α(N)).

remember.formula:
components = union-find over roads
for each component of size s:
    cost += min(s * c_lib,                      # a library in every city
                c_lib + (s - 1) * c_road)       # one library, span with roads
answer = sum of per-component costs
rules: Every component needs **at least one** library — a city with no library can never reach one through roads alone.
If `c_lib ≤ c_road`, libraries are never worse than roads — the answer is just `n * c_lib`. State this special case first.
Spanning a component of `s` cities needs exactly `s − 1` roads (a spanning tree); extra roads are wasted money.
Decide each component **independently** — roads only connect cities already in the same component, so components never share cost.
Use `long` for the running total: `n` up to 10⁵ times costs up to 10⁵ overflows 32-bit `int`.
whenToUse: Cost is split between a 'node cost' and an 'edge cost' and you must cover every node
The graph breaks into independent pieces you can price separately
You only need connectivity (reach a facility), not actual shortest distances
The decision per group is a simple two-way greedy comparison
antiSignals: You need the actual shortest path between two cities → BFS / Dijkstra, not components
Edges carry differing weights you must minimize over → that is an MST (Kruskal/Prim), not this flat comparison
You must keep the graph connected as a whole → spanning-tree problem, not per-component
Libraries have per-city differing costs → this uniform-cost greedy no longer applies
remember.takeaway: When a problem splits cleanly into independent groups, price each group on its own and add the results. Here the only graph work is 'which cities are connected', which Union-Find answers in near-constant time per edge — the rest is a one-line cost comparison.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that the graph decomposes into independent connected components and that each component reduces to a tiny greedy choice, rather than reaching for an expensive shortest-path or MST routine.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Forgetting that every component still needs one library even when roads are cheaper, or using a 32-bit int for the total and overflowing on large inputs.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call out the `c_lib ≤ c_road` shortcut immediately, derive 'span s cities with s − 1 roads' as a spanning tree, and explain why components are independent so the costs simply add.

problemStatement:
The HackerLand government wants every citizen to have access to a library. There are `n` cities (numbered `1` to `n`) and a list of bidirectional `roads` that could be repaired, where `roads[i] = [u, v]` means a road can be repaired between city `u` and city `v`.

Building a library in a city costs `c_lib`. Repairing one road costs `c_road`. A city has access to a library if it contains one, or if it is connected through repaired roads to a city that contains one.

Return the **minimum total cost** to give every city access to a library.
constraints: Roads are bidirectional; the graph may be disconnected
The answer can exceed 32-bit range — use 64-bit
understanding: Each city must end up linked (directly or via roads) to at least one library. Roads only matter inside a group of cities that the road list connects. Within one such group you pay for exactly one library and then choose the cheaper of 'a library everywhere' versus 'one library plus enough roads to reach the rest'. Different groups never interact, so total cost is the sum of each group's own cheapest plan.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the cities 1-indexed or 0-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The HackerRank statement uses 1..n. Internally I will shift to 0-based for array-backed Union-Find and shift back only at the boundary.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same road appear twice, or can there be self-loops?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Duplicate roads and self-loops are harmless — Union-Find ignores an edge whose endpoints already share a root, so no extra cost is added.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must the whole map be connected at the end?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Each component is solved on its own; an isolated city just gets its own library.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is it ever right to repair more than s − 1 roads in a component of size s?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Never. s − 1 roads already connect all s cities (a spanning tree). Any extra road only adds cost without improving access.

examples.explanation: All 3 cities form one component. Roads are cheaper (1 < 2): one library (2) + (3−1) roads (2×1=2) = 4. Building 3 libraries would cost 6.
Libraries are cheaper (2 ≤ 5), so ignore roads and build a library in every city: 6 × 2 = 12.
Component {1,2,3,4} size 4: min(4×6, 6 + 3×1) = min(24, 9) = 9. City 5 is alone: 6. Total 9 + 6 = 15.

approaches.name: DFS / BFS Component Sizing (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first as the most direct way to get component sizes — a flood fill over an adjacency list. It is just as correct as Union-Find; the cost formula is identical.
hints: Strip away the cost question for a moment. What you really need from the graph is: how many cities are in each connected group?
Build an adjacency list, then walk every unvisited city, flood-filling its whole component and counting how many cities you touch.
For each component size s you collect, add min(s × c_lib, c_lib + (s − 1) × c_road) to the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the adjacency list is O(N + E). Each vertex and edge is visited once during the traversal, so the flood fill is O(N + E). The cost arithmetic per component is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
The graph problem hidden inside this question is simply *component sizing*. Once you know how many cities sit in each connected group, the money question is pure arithmetic.

**Why a flood fill gives the sizes.** Start at any unvisited city and walk every city reachable from it through roads, marking each visited and counting as you go. When the walk stalls, you have one full component and its size. Pick the next unvisited city and repeat. Every city is reached exactly once, so the sizes you collect partition all `n` cities.

**Why the traversal must be iterative here.** With up to `10⁵` cities a recursive DFS can nest `10⁵` frames deep on a long chain of roads and overflow the call stack. Use an explicit stack (or a queue for BFS) so the depth lives in the heap, not the call stack. The order of visiting does not matter — DFS and BFS both produce the same component sizes.

**Why the cost is per-component and additive.** A road can only ever join two cities that are already in the same component (that is what a road *does*). So no spending in one component can help another, and the global minimum is just the sum of each component's own minimum. Inside a component of size `s` you compare two complete plans: a library in all `s` cities, or a single library plus the `s − 1` roads that connect the rest to it.
approaches.insight: The whole problem is 'find component sizes, then apply a fixed two-line formula'. Recognizing that the cost decomposes per component is the real insight — the traversal is just bookkeeping.

pitfalls: Recursive DFS on a 10⁵-city chain — stack overflow. Use an explicit stack or BFS.
Adding only one direction of each road — splits a component in two and overprices it.
Computing size × c_lib in 32-bit int — overflows around 2×10⁹.

approaches.name: Union-Find Component Sizing (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The cleanest answer when you only need connectivity, not paths. Phrase it as 'union each road's endpoints, then read off component sizes from the roots'.
hints: You never need the actual roads after grouping — only which cities ended up together. What structure answers 'are these two in the same group?' in near-constant time?
Union-Find: union the two endpoints of every road, with path compression and union by rank. After processing all roads, the size of each root's set is its component size.
Walk every city, find its root, and tally how many cities map to each root. Then apply min(s × c_lib, c_lib + (s − 1) × c_road) per root.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each union and find is O(α(N)) — the inverse Ackermann function, effectively constant. E roads give O(E · α(N)); the final sweep over N cities to read sizes is O(N · α(N)). Space is O(N) for the parent and size arrays.
approaches.explanation:
Union-Find (a disjoint-set forest) is the tool when the *only* question about the graph is 'which things are connected'. It never materializes paths, so it sidesteps all traversal and the stack-depth worry entirely.

**How the grouping works.** Each city starts as its own set. For every road `[u, v]` you `union` the two endpoints — merging their sets if they differ. After all roads are processed, two cities share a root exactly when a chain of roads connects them. The `size[]` array, carried on each root, then tells you how big each component is.

**Why union by rank plus path compression matters.** A naïve `find` that walks parents to the root can degrade to `O(N)` on a skewed tree, making the whole run `O(N·E)`. Path compression flattens the tree during `find` (pointing nodes at their grandparent), and union by rank attaches the shorter tree under the taller one. Together they pin each operation at `O(α(N))`, which is at most 4 for any input you will ever see — effectively constant.

**Why the find loop is iterative.** `find` climbs parent pointers in a `while` loop, never recursing. On `10⁵` cities that avoids any chance of a deep recursive call blowing the stack — the same defensive choice as the iterative DFS, applied to the set-find.

**Reading the answer.** Sweep all `n` cities, find each city's root, and accumulate the count per root. Each distinct root is one component of some size `s`, and you add `min(s × c_lib, c_lib + (s − 1) × c_road)` for it. Sum across roots for the total. The `c_lib ≤ c_road` shortcut still applies — when libraries are cheaper, every component picks the `s × c_lib` branch and the total collapses to `n × c_lib`.
approaches.insight: Union-Find is the reflex whenever a problem is purely about connectivity with no need for distances or paths. It turns the graph into a near-constant-time 'same group?' oracle, leaving only the O(1)-per-component cost formula to finish the job.

pitfalls: Dropping the per-component library — a component of size s with only roads has no library to reach.
Recursive find on a long chain — risks stack overflow; the iterative while loop avoids it.
Accumulating the total in 32-bit int — n × c_lib can reach 10¹⁰, well past int range.
Counting size off non-root nodes — only the root carries the correct component size.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that every component needs at least one library even when roads are cheaper.
Using a 32-bit int for the running total and overflowing on large n × cost.
Recursing in DFS or find and overflowing the call stack on a 10⁵-node chain.
Repairing more than s − 1 roads in a component, paying for redundant edges.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Skipping the mandatory per-component library
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When roads are cheaper, candidates sometimes price a component as (s − 1) × c_road and forget the one library that makes the roads worth anything. Without a library, a connected component still has zero access.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
# roads cheaper, but no library bought
total += (size - 1) * c_road
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
# one library anchors the component, roads reach the rest
total += c_lib + (size - 1) * c_road

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With n up to 10⁵ and costs up to 10⁵, a single component can cost on the order of 10¹⁰, which silently wraps around in a 32-bit int and yields a negative or tiny answer.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int total = 0;
total += size * cLib;          // size * cLib overflows int
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
long total = 0;
total += (long) size * cLib;   // promote before multiplying

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursive find / DFS blowing the stack
commonMistakesDetailed.why: A path of 10⁵ cities forms a chain that deep. Recursive find or DFS nests one frame per node and overflows the call stack; an explicit loop keeps the depth in the heap.

patternNote: Connected Components + Independent Per-Group Greedy. Recognize it when a graph splits into pieces you can price separately and each piece reduces to a small comparison. Union-Find supplies the component sizes in near-constant time per edge; the same skeleton appears in Components in a Graph, Number of Provinces, and Journey to the Moon.
